title: Terpenes in Plain English | The Bridge
description: That smell when the jar opens is chemistry you can use. What terpenes are, what research says about sativa and indica labels, and why the aroma fades.
lede: That smell when the jar opens is chemistry you can actually use. Just don't let anybody sell it to you as a guarantee.
html:
Open a jar and your nose starts working before you've read a word of the label. What it's reading is terpenes: naturally occurring compounds found in practically all plant life, similar to essential oils, and responsible for how cannabis smells and part of how it tastes. A 2020 review in Molecules counts hundreds identified in cannabis. The plant makes them in the same place it makes cannabinoids: the glandular trichomes, the tiny resin glands found in highest density on female flowers.

Four you can smell for

You've met these outside a dispensary. New York's regulator gives four easy reference points:

  • Limonene: citrus.
  • Pinene: pine.
  • Linalool: lavender.
  • Caryophyllene: black pepper.

The journal pages in the state's guide also list myrcene and humulene, so expect to see those names around too.

What they do to the word on the jar

Now the part that unsettles the menu. A 2021 study in Nature Plants re-analyzed 297 samples, genotyped 137 of them and compared the results with the sativa and indica labels they came with. Across the genome, samples labelled sativa and indica were genetically indistinct. What did track with the labels was a small set of aromatic compounds. Myrcene leaned indica. Bergamotene and farnesene, with their tea-like and fruity aromas, leaned sativa. The authors' working hypothesis is that growers and breeders have been assigning those labels largely by aroma.

None of this throws out the vocabulary on our Facts page. Sativa, indica and hybrid are still how the plant's story gets told, and knowing the three base types is a fine way to start. The state's guide uses them too, then adds that these three terms alone aren't enough to tell you which of the hundreds of combinations you're holding. It also warns that a cultivar in one state might be totally different in another, even with the same name. Terpenes are the next layer of detail.

What they might do to you

Go carefully here, because this is where sales copy outruns science. The state's guide says some research indicates terpenes have the potential to influence the effects of cannabis by interacting with cannabinoids, and that researchers are studying the idea under the name entourage effect. The Nature Plants authors cite evidence that a terpene profile affects psychoactive properties. The 2020 review says those interactions have so far only been speculated on. The guide does float that linalool might make you sleepy and limonene might invigorate you. Notice the word might. Nobody can promise you a feeling from a line on a lab report.

Why the smell fades

Terpenes are volatile, a chemist's way of saying they leave. In a 2020 storage study in Frontiers in Plant Science, terpenoid levels fell under every storage condition the team tested, and after four months all of the ground samples ran lower than their whole counterparts. A jar that has gone quiet is telling you something. It's also a good reason to store flower well and buy what you'll actually finish.

Using this at the shop

  1. Check the label and the lab report for a terpene profile, if one is available.
  2. Write down the cultivar, the THC figure and the top two or three terpenes.
  3. Afterward, note how it went. The state's guide has journal pages for this.
  4. Change one thing at a time. Switch everything at once and you learn nothing.

Your nose plus your notes will teach you more than a strain name will. The flower shelf is a good place to begin.
